title: Why our first game is a sort puzzle: picking a mobile game category with research, not instinct
excerpt: How we chose what kind of mobile game to build: the rule that crowded only matters relative to growth, why sort puzzles beat block puzzles for a small studio, the ideas we rejected, and why the jars are full of spice.
content:
SpiceCraft is our first game. It is a sorting puzzle set in a spice mill: tap a jar, tap another, and the first jar lifts, travels across and pours. Keep going until every jar holds a single spice. It went live on Google Play in October 2026, and the iPhone version is in Apple's review.

Before a single jar was drawn, we spent a day on a question most small studios answer by instinct: **what kind of game should we build at all?**

This post is the answer, and how we got to it. It covers the rule that decided it, the numbers behind it, the five ideas we investigated and threw away, and why a category with a billion downloads still had room for one more game. It is the first of a five-part series on how SpiceCraft was built.

### A short glossary

- **Category (or subgenre):** a family of games that share one core rule, such as "sort colours into containers" or "fit blocks into a grid".
- **Hypercasual:** very simple games paid for by ads only. Tap to jump, avoid the obstacle, repeat.
- **Hybrid-casual:** the same simple loop, plus progression and a few optional purchases or rewards.
- **ARPDAU:** average revenue per daily active user. How much money one player brings in on one day, averaged across everyone who played that day.
- **Rewarded video:** an ad the player *chooses* to watch, in exchange for something in the game, such as a hint.
- **Interstitial:** a full-screen ad shown between levels, which the player did not ask for.
- **eCPM:** what advertisers pay for a thousand ad views. Higher is better for the game maker.
- **Live-ops:** running events, sales and new content continuously after launch. Expensive, and the main advantage big publishers have.

## Start with what you can actually win

We are a small studio. For this project that meant one engineer, a fixed number of build hours a week, and no marketing budget. That ruled out a lot before any research started.

So the question was never "what is the most popular game?". It was **"where can a small team with good taste and no ad budget get a fair hearing?"** Those are different questions, and they give different answers.

### Hypercasual is closing; hybrid-casual is open

The first thing the research showed was that pure hypercasual games, the ad-only kind, are in structural decline. Installs are falling while the cost of buying each player is rising, and the margin has closed for anyone without a large advertising operation already running.

Hybrid-casual keeps the same simple loop and adds light progression and optional rewards. That one change moves revenue per player by roughly ten times:

| Genre | ARPDAU (revenue per player per day) |
| --- | --- |
| Hypercasual, ads only | $0.02 to $0.05 |
| Hybrid-casual | $0.15 to $0.50 |
| Mid-core | $0.20 to $1.00 |
| Top strategy and RPG | $1.50 and up |

Hybrid-casual was also the only ad-driven segment whose in-app purchase revenue grew in 2025, up 20% to $4.2 billion according to [Deconstructor of Fun](https://www.deconstructoroffun.com/blog/2026/2/2/state-of-mobile-2026), with puzzle games leading it. So the target was a hybrid-casual puzzle game. The harder question was which one.

## The rule that decided everything

Every puzzle category on the app stores is crowded. If "crowded" were a reason to stay away, there would be nowhere to go. So we needed a sharper rule, and this is the one we settled on:

> **Saturation only means something relative to growth.**

![Diagram: mobile puzzle categories in three groups. Crowded and growing, which is enterable: block, sort, screw, merge, jigsaw, tile match. Crowded and flat, which looks open but is not: sudoku, nonogram, mahjong, classic solitaire, mature match-3. Crowded with a moat: solitaire, where one company holds 63% of spend.](/blog/spicecraft/01-market-map.svg)

There are three kinds of crowded, and only one of them is worth entering.

**Crowded and growing.** New players are arriving every day who have no favourite yet. Store rankings keep reshuffling, and a good new game can catch some of that flow. Block puzzles, sort puzzles, screw puzzles, merge, jigsaw and tile-match were all here.

**Crowded and flat.** No new demand is arriving, so the leaders' half-million reviews and ten years of store ranking are permanent. There is never a moment when the charts reshuffle in your favour. Sudoku, nonograms, mahjong, classic solitaire and mature match-3 were here.

This second case is the dangerous one, and it is worth saying why. In a flat category no single game dominates, so it **looks** open. It is not. The reviews and rankings of the existing games are a wall, and nothing is coming along to knock it down.

**Crowded with a moat.** One well-funded company holds the category with live-ops and marketing nobody small can match. Solitaire is the clear example: Playtika holds 63% of all solitaire spending. At least this case is easy to see.

Once you sort categories this way, most of the obvious "easy, safe" choices fall out immediately. Sudoku and nonograms are the safest possible builds, and they were on our early shortlist. They came off it because they are crowded **and** flat, the one combination with no way in.

## Comparing the categories that were left

For each remaining category we wrote down how it makes money, how hard it is for a small team to build, how much new content it needs forever, and one proof point that real money is being made:

| Category | How hard to build | Content it needs | Proof point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Block puzzle | Easy to medium | None | Block Blast in the top two grossing; Color Block Jam at $42M a quarter |
| Sort puzzle | Easy | None, levels can be generated | About 1 billion downloads and $280M in 2025, up 176% |
| Screw puzzle | Easy to medium | None | Screwdom at $27.1M a quarter |
| Tile-match | Easy to medium | Icon art | Tile Explorer at $200K a month |
| Jigsaw | Easy to medium | A constant supply of images | Downloads up 21%, mostly players over 45 |
| Merge | Medium to hard | Art plus a full economy | $1.3B in the first half of 2026 |
| Hidden object | Avoid | A new story chapter every week | A large team behind each leader |

The "content it needs" column matters more than it looks. A game that needs new art or new story every week is a game that needs a team every week. A game whose levels can be generated by a program can keep going on one person's time.

That left two serious candidates: **block puzzle** and **sort puzzle**.

## Why sort beat block puzzle

On paper, block puzzle is the better game. We said so in our notes at the time, and it is still true:

- **A better loop.** An endless scoring run never runs out of content, while a level-based game always eventually does.
- **More money per player.** "Continue after you lose" is the strongest single hook in casual games.
- **A bigger prize.** The category leader makes tens of millions of dollars a quarter.

We still chose sort, and the reason was the **shape** of each market, not its size.

### Who gets the money

In block puzzle, one game is a global top-20 download with enormous brand recognition. The only real way to compete is marketing spend. The likely outcomes are huge or nothing, and a small studio with no budget gets nothing.

Sort puzzles are different. According to [Naavik's analysis of puzzle subgenres](https://naavik.co/digest/how-niche-subgenres-are-reshaping-the-mobile-puzzle-market/), sort has "healthy, gradual revenue distribution across many games simultaneously". The leader, Magic Sort, took only **18%** of the subgenre's revenue, while many other games each earn $5 to 15 million a year. In most categories the leader takes 60% or more.

That is an unusual and very friendly structure for a newcomer. **A category where nobody can win outright is a category where you do not have to win.** You only have to be good enough to be one of the many.

### Why sort spreads out like that

Our best explanation, and it is an inference rather than a measurement, is that sort is a **format**, not a game. The puzzle underneath is identical whether the things being sorted are water, balls, screws or goods on a shelf. Nobody's version can be dramatically better, only different. So players spread across many games instead of all moving to one.

Compare match-3, where the leading game genuinely is better than a generic match-3 because of everything layered on top, and the market has consolidated hard around it.

That also told us where our effort should go. If no version of the rules can be much better, then **theme, craft and difficulty tuning** are what set one game apart. Those are things taste buys, not things money buys. For a studio with taste and no ad budget, that is exactly the right fight.

## Why sort makes money without being pushy

The second reason was how naturally sort games earn from ads.

In most games, you have to invent a reason for someone to want to watch a rewarded video. In a sort puzzle, the game creates the moment by itself: players regularly get stuck, with no good move left. At that exact moment, a few things are obviously valuable to them, such as one more empty jar, a hint, or a few more moves. They are stuck, they want out, and a short video solves it.

That matters for money, because rewarded video pays far more than ads the player did not ask for:

| Ad format | eCPM in top markets (per 1,000 views) |
| --- | --- |
| Rewarded video | $10 to $30 |
| Interstitial | $0.50 to $1.50 |

It also matters for fairness. A rewarded video is the player's choice, offered at a moment when they actually want what is on offer. We liked building a game that earns most from the ads players choose, rather than the ones forced on them. In SpiceCraft every helper behind a video is optional, and no level ever requires one. (There is also a full-screen ad roughly every fourth level, never straight after another ad, and never when you have just run out of moves. That is the one ad a player does not choose.)

## The ideas we threw away

The most useful part of the research document is not the winner. It is the list of rejected ideas, each with the reason, so nobody has to rediscover them. Here are the main ones.

### The arrows puzzle that topped the world charts

In the second quarter of 2026, *Arrows - Puzzle Escape* was the most-downloaded mobile game in the world, with more than 110 million lifetime downloads. It looked like the obvious thing to chase.

The month-by-month numbers told a different story:

| Month | Downloads | Global rank |
| --- | --- | --- |
| June 2026 | 25M+ | Top 5 |
| July 2026 | 11.4M | #11 |
| August 2026 | Under 8.6M | Out of the top 20 |

That is a classic hypercasual spike: about two months at the peak, then halving every month. The original game is still well rated and still updated, so it is not dead. But the category was no longer bringing in new players, which is the only reason to enter a hot category. The copies that were winning came from large publishers, and a snake-themed version of the same idea already had around a dozen near-identical clones.

**Lesson:** a chart-topper tells you where demand **was**. The trend tells you where it is going.

### The path puzzle with great retention

LinkedIn's daily *Zip* puzzle (draw one path through numbered cells that fills the whole grid) has real demand. LinkedIn reported that 84% of Zip players come back the next day.

But that demand did not turn into app installs. The most successful standalone copy we found had about 74,000 lifetime downloads, and the long-time leader of the closest category earns tens of thousands of dollars a month after thirteen years. People were happy playing it free in a browser.

We also caught a mistake in our own draft here. An early version used "arrow and path puzzles are rising" as support for this idea. That was wrong: the arrows game above is a sliding-tile game, not a path puzzle. The two categories just share a word. We wrote the correction into the document rather than quietly deleting the line.

### Sudoku and nonograms

Safe, simple to build, and crowded and flat. They were on the list, then off it, for the reason explained above.

### A memory jigsaw

The idea: show a picture for 15 to 20 seconds, hide it, then make the player rebuild it. It had two problems. Jigsaw's growth comes from players looking for something calm, and a memory test under pressure is exactly what that audience is avoiding. And memory does not really help with a jigsaw anyway, because you assemble one piece against its neighbour, not from a memory of the whole picture.

## What it costs to try

Part of the decision was being honest about money. With both app store accounts already paid for, almost every tool a first game needs has a free tier it will not outgrow:

- **Unity** is free until revenue and funding both pass $200,000.
- **AdMob** (Google's ad network) has no fee; Google takes a share of ad revenue.
- **Store commission** is 15%, not 30%, under Apple's Small Business Program and Google's first-million-dollar tier.

The one cost that grows with ambition is buying players through ads. Everything else stays close to free at our size. We also wrote down some honest expectations: most solo mobile releases earn tens to low hundreds of dollars a month, and what separates the rare big success is a loop people return to plus a way to reach players you already own. Not code quality.

### Why Unity, when our house language is Flutter

Most of our apps are built in Flutter. For this game we chose Unity anyway, because it is the engine with official, vendor-maintained plugins for the ad networks a free game depends on. We also decided to use **AdMob alone** until the game has roughly 50,000 daily players. Connecting several ad networks at once ("mediation") is real complexity, and at small scale it pays nothing back.

## Rebuild the rules, never the look

A sort puzzle is a well-known mechanic, and we were not the first to build one. So we checked where the line is.

Game rules are generally not protected by copyright. Art, music, sound effects, names and the exact layout of a game's screens are. Our rule was simple: **rebuild mechanics, never presentation.** We did study the motion of another sort game's pour, beat by beat, and summed up the rule for that study in four words: "steal order, not art". The other studio's art and screen recording were never even added to our code repository.

Every jar, colour, sound and screen in SpiceCraft is our own.

## Why spices

So we had a category where the rules are shared and the look is the main way to stand out. Then we looked at what the category actually looks like.

Almost every sort game on the stores is cold glass, clear liquid and clinical laboratory lighting. Test tubes and beakers, again and again, across a billion downloads. That is a visual rut, and it was the opening: **build a warm one.**

We wrote down what a good theme needed:

1. **Recognisable with no explanation.** The goal should be clear from one screenshot.
2. **Visually different from glass and water.**
3. **A satisfying motion**, because the pour happens hundreds of times a session.
4. **Room for sound**, since sort games are mostly played with sound on.
5. **Not already taken.** Water, balls, screws, hoops and goods on shelves all were.

Then we listed places people sort things in real life, from laundry to sewing boxes to bakery counters, and narrowed it to four: thread spools, an ice-cream parlour, buttons in a tin, and a **spice kitchen**.

Spice won on warmth and on colour. Jars of ground spice on a counter (turmeric yellow, chilli red, cumin brown, cardamom green, saffron orange) stand out hard against a wall of blue-glass competitors. Powder also settles rather than sloshes, which is a different, more satisfying motion to animate. And it has a story we wanted to tell. Indian kitchens keep masala in steel and ceramic tins you cannot see into, and that detail went on to become a real game mechanic.

The default scene became a **spice mill**: dark brushed steel with light pooling on one side. Saturated spice against a dark, cool background has far more punch than the same colours on cream.

## A theme is not a game

A warm look gets someone to install. It does not make them stay. Our notes said it bluntly: "a straight sort clone is a prototype, not a product".

So we set a rule for every new feature. **It has to change what fails, or what the goal is. Not just what things look like.** SpiceCraft shipped with four of these:

![Diagram: SpiceCraft's four mechanics. Jars of 3, 4 or 5 change what counts as finished. Ceramic jars hide what is under the top spice, changing what you know. Masala recipe bowls change the goal itself. A move budget instead of a timer changes what fails.](/blog/spicecraft/01-four-flavours.svg)

1. **Jars of different sizes.** Jars hold 3, 4 or 5 and are drawn at their real height. That breaks the assumption every sort player has, that any full jar is finished.
2. **Ceramic jars.** You can see the spice on top, but not what is underneath. The puzzle goes from perfect information to partial information, which raises difficulty far more than adding colours does.
3. **Masala recipe bowls.** A brass bowl wants spices in a set order. Every other sort game asks "make each container pure". This one asks a second question on the same board.
4. **A move budget instead of a timer.** Nothing rushes you, but every pour counts.

Each of these deserves a post of its own, and two of the coming ones go deep: how we guarantee all 200 levels can be finished, and how the move budget, stars and hints stay fair.

### Ideas we cut on purpose

The same notes list what we deliberately left out of the first version: accounts, a backend, daily challenges, leaderboards and virtual currencies. "Not later, not if there is time. Cut." A smaller game with a good difficulty curve beats a bigger game with a bad one.

## What we would tell another small studio

1. **Ask where you can win, not what is popular.** The two questions have different answers.
2. **Crowded is fine if the category is growing.** Crowded and flat looks open and is not.
3. **Look at who gets the money, not how much there is.** An 18% leader share is an invitation. A 63% share is a wall.
4. **A chart-topper is a rear-view mirror.** Read the month-by-month trend.
5. **Write down what you rejected, and why.** Ours stopped at least three good-looking ideas from coming back.
6. **In a category where the rules are shared, taste is the differentiator.** Spend it on theme, feel and fairness.

SpiceCraft is free on [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.spicecraft), and the iPhone version is coming soon. If you play, we would love to know which level stopped you.

Next in this series: [200 levels, every one solvable](/blog/spicecraft-200-levels-every-one-solvable), on how the levels are generated, checked by a solver and arranged into a difficulty curve.

title: 200 levels, every one solvable: how SpiceCraft generates, proves and orders its puzzles
excerpt: Inside SpiceCraft's level pipeline: shuffle-then-prove generation, a depth-first solver with a carefully chosen state key, proven minimum moves, robot players that measure difficulty, and a drawn difficulty curve, all reproducible from one seed.
content:
SpiceCraft ships with 200 levels. Every one of them has been solved by a program before it ever reached a phone, and solved in the **fewest possible moves**, proven, not estimated. The number of moves each level gives you is set from that proven minimum.

That is the promise behind a line on our store page: every level can be finished.

This post explains how that promise is kept. It walks through the pipeline that makes the levels: how a board is dealt, how a solver proves it can be won, how we find the shortest solution, how "robot players" of different strengths measure how hard it is, and how 200 boards are arranged into a difficulty curve that rises the way we drew it. It is part two of our series on building SpiceCraft.

If you have not played a sort puzzle: a board is a row of jars holding layers of coloured spice. You pour from one jar into another, and a pour is only allowed onto the same spice or into an empty jar. You win when every jar holds a single spice.

### A short glossary

- **Solver:** a program that tries moves until it finds a way to win, or proves there is none.
- **State (or position):** one arrangement of spice in the jars.
- **Search:** exploring positions move by move. Each position looked at is called a **node**.
- **Depth-first search:** a search that follows one line of moves as deep as it goes before backing up and trying another.
- **Node budget:** the most positions a search may look at before it gives up and says "I don't know".
- **Seed:** a number that fixes a random number generator, so the same seed always produces the same "random" results.
- **Par:** the target number of moves for three stars.
- **Move budget:** how many moves the level gives you before you run out.
- **Tier:** a difficulty label: Easy, Easy-medium, Medium, Medium-hard, Hard and Hard-plus (shown in the game as "Xhard").

## Levels are made offline, not on the phone

The first decision shapes everything else: **levels are never generated on the player's phone.** They are generated, measured and assembled on a development machine, then shipped inside the game as data files, 100 levels each in two packs.

That lets the pipeline be as slow and careful as it needs to be. It can search millions of positions per board, throw away thousands of candidates, and run a full audit afterwards. The phone only ever runs a few small, bounded searches during play, which we come back to at the end.

![Diagram: the SpiceCraft level pipeline. Shuffle and deal a board, prove it solvable, find its proven minimum moves, set par and a move budget, let robot players of increasing strength measure its difficulty, add it to a pool, then fill a drawn difficulty curve by nearest score, and audit the result.](/blog/spicecraft/02-level-pipeline.svg)

## The rules, written as code

A pipeline that proves things about levels needs the rules written down exactly. In SpiceCraft they live in a small C# library with no dependency on the Unity engine, so they can be tested in seconds without opening the game.

A board holds a list of vessels (glass jars, ceramic jars, and sometimes the masala bowl), plus a few facts about the level. The rules for a pour are short:

```csharp
var amount = run < destination.Room ? run : destination.Room;
return PourCheck.Allowed(amount, spice);
```

A pour moves the **whole run** of matching spice off the top of a jar, capped by the room in the destination. The destination must be empty or have the same spice on top. A finished jar cannot be poured from, and nothing ever pours out of the masala bowl.

### The bug that taught us "home"

One rule needs special attention, because getting it wrong broke the game quietly.

SpiceCraft has jars of three sizes: 3, 4 and 5. Early on, a jar counted as finished when it was full and held only one spice. Then a spice with **five** units filled a **four**-unit jar. It looked finished, sealed itself, and left its fifth unit stranded somewhere else. The board was now impossible to win, and nothing on screen said so.

The fix was to give every spice a **home size**: the size of jar that spice must fill. A jar is complete only when it is full, uniform, **and** its size equals that spice's home size:

```csharp
vessel.IsFull && vessel.IsUniform && board.Home[vessel[0].Value] == vessel.Capacity
```

The home size is stored with the level, never worked out from how many units exist. That distinction (how big the jar must be, versus how much spice there is) is now the first thing anyone working on the rules is told, and the original bug ships as a named regression test.

### Two flavours the rules have to know about

- **Ceramic jars** hide everything below the top spice. Hiding changes what the **player knows**, never what is **legal**. A layer becomes visible once it has been on top, and stays visible.
- **The masala bowl** accepts only the next spice its recipe wants, and only as many units as the recipe asks for. A wrong spice is refused rather than spoiling the bowl, which keeps every board provably solvable. Spices used in a recipe get one spare unit, so finishing the recipe never makes a jar unfillable.

## Making a board: shuffle, deal, then prove

The obvious way to make a solvable puzzle is to start from a solved board and scramble it with moves played backwards. Then it must be solvable, because you can just play the scramble forwards.

We tried it, and it does not work for sort puzzles. On a solved board, every jar is full of one spice, so the only legal move is onto an empty jar. The "scramble" barely scrambles anything.

So SpiceCraft does the opposite. **Deal randomly, then prove it.**

1. Give each spice exactly as many units as its home jar holds, so the solved arrangement always exists.
2. Shuffle all the units with a seeded random generator and deal them into the jars.
3. Reject the deal if it is already solved, or if **any** jar starts complete. Every jar on screen should need at least one pour.
4. Ask the solver. Only a board the solver proves winnable goes on, and only then are some jars chosen to be ceramic.
5. Try again, up to 500 deals per candidate.

## The solver

The solver answers one question about a board, with one of three answers: **solvable**, **unsolvable**, or **budget exceeded** (it looked at too many positions without deciding).

### Depth-first, with a memory

It is a depth-first search: play a pour, then another, as deep as possible, and back up when stuck. It remembers every position it has already explored, so it never explores the same one twice.

A few details make it fast enough to run millions of times:

- **An explicit stack** instead of recursive function calls, so a deep search cannot overflow.
- **Make and unmake:** instead of copying the whole board for every move, it applies a pour, explores, then reverses the pour on the same private copy.
- **A node budget:** two million positions during generation. If a board needs more, the answer is "budget exceeded", and the board is thrown away.

We chose depth-first over breadth-first search (exploring all positions one move away, then all positions two moves away, and so on) on purpose. Breadth-first has to keep every position at the current distance in memory at once, and on these boards that explodes.

### The key that decides what "the same position" means

Remembering positions needs a way to tell when two positions are the same. This turned out to be the riskiest piece of code in the whole project.

Two boards that only differ in the order of their jars are the same puzzle: jar order on the shelf does not matter. So the natural key is "sort the jars, then compare". Our first prototype did exactly that, sorting **all** jars together.

That stopped being correct the moment jars came in different sizes and kinds. Swapping the contents of a three-unit jar and a five-unit jar gives a genuinely different puzzle. So does swapping a glass jar's contents with a ceramic jar's. A key that treats them as equal can wrongly skip a real position, and either call a winnable board unwinnable, or "prove" a board winnable through a move that is not legal.

So the key sorts jars **only within groups of the same size and kind**, and keeps the bowl in a group of its own:

![Diagram: how the solver decides two positions are the same. Jars are grouped by size and kind (glass 3, glass 4, ceramic 4, glass 5, bowl), sorted only within each group, then joined into one key. Sorting all jars together would wrongly treat a 3-jar and a 5-jar holding the same spice as interchangeable.](/blog/spicecraft/02-state-key.svg)

What is deliberately left **out** of the key is which hidden layers have been revealed. That is about what the player knows, not about the puzzle itself.

### Finding the shortest route, and proving it

Knowing a board can be won is not enough. To set par and the move budget fairly, we need the **fewest** moves it can be won in.

A plain depth-first search finds *a* route, but rarely the shortest. So the minimum is found in two steps:

1. Run the ordinary search to get **some** route. Its length is an upper limit.
2. Run searches that are only allowed a fixed number of moves, starting from a **lower limit** and going up one at a time: "can it be won in 12? in 13? in 14?". The first limit that succeeds is the true minimum.

Each limited search also skips any line of play that cannot possibly finish within its limit, using a quick estimate of how many pours are still needed at least. For each spice, it compares how many separate runs the spice is split into now with how many it will be in at the end, takes at least one pour if the spice is not finished yet, and adds those up across spices. That estimate never overshoots, which is what makes the answer exact.

We added that estimate after a real failure. The first full generation run shipped twelve **estimated** minimums on the biggest boards, because the search ran out of budget before proving them. One of them claimed 84 moves on a board whose near-identical neighbour was proven at 24.

The rule that came out of it is strict: **a board whose minimum cannot be proven exact does not ship.** Today all 200 levels carry a proven minimum.

### What about hidden spice?

The solver sees the true board, including what is inside the ceramic jars. That is right for the question it answers ("can this be won at all?"), because hiding never changes what is legal.

How hard the hidden jars make a level **for a person** is a different question, and it is answered by the robots in the next section.

## Measuring difficulty with robots

How hard is a level? The obvious measures (number of colours, number of jars, length of the solution) turned out to be poor guides. Our notes put it bluntly: "volume is bookkeeping". A board with many jars can be easy, and a small one can be cruel.

So difficulty is **measured by playing**. A ladder of robot players, each stronger than the last, attempts every candidate board inside the same move budget a person would get:

| Robot | How it plays |
| --- | --- |
| R1, R2 | Greedy: picks the best-looking pour right now, with no look-ahead |
| R3 | Looks 3 pours ahead |
| R4 | Looks 6 pours ahead |
| R5 | Looks 12 pours ahead |
| R6 | Plays perfectly (the full solver) |

A level's tier is set by the **weakest robot that wins at least 80% of 50 attempts** inside the budget. A board an R1 can beat is Easy. A board only R6 can beat is as hard as anything we ship.

Hidden jars get their own robots. These "belief" robots only know what a player could have seen: the layers that have been revealed, remembered perfectly but with no guessing. A board's tier is the harder of the two ladders, the one that sees everything and the one that only sees what you see.

### Traps

The robots also measure **traps**: pours that look fine but make the board unwinnable. For each board we record how many pours can be played safely from the start, how dense the traps are, and how long a trap takes to "bite" (become obvious).

Those numbers feed the tier rules. Easy boards must have at least 12 safe opening pours, for example, so a new player cannot lose a level on their third tap without knowing why.

### Hard levels need a fair way to see

On the two hardest tiers, undo is switched off. That raised a fairness problem straight away: a ceramic jar you cannot see into, with no undo, is not a hard puzzle. Our notes call it "a coin flip wearing difficulty's clothes".

So a Hard or Xhard level must have something the optional Peek can reveal. If it does not, its tier is capped lower. Turning undo off first exposed that 15 of 22 hard levels at the time were all-glass, which led to new kinds of boards being generated for those slots.

## Par, the move budget and stars

Once a board's minimum is proven:

- **Par** is the minimum plus 2.
- **The move budget** is par times 1.25, rounded, plus 2 moves for each ceramic jar (hidden spice costs moves to discover) and 2 for each recipe slot.
- **Three stars** means finishing at or under par. **Two stars** means finishing under par times 1.2. Anything else that wins is **one star**.

The very first boards a new player sees get a gentler budget (par times 1.5, and 3 moves per ceramic jar), but only if the weakest robots can beat them with it. On the shipped levels that is exactly the first six.

These numbers changed after real play. Our first budgets gave roughly twice the shortest route on every tier. A player who finished all of the first hundred levels told us the moves were "always too much". So the budget formula was tightened: the average budget dropped from 32 moves to 25, and, because budgets only change the money and not the board, **not a single level changed tier**.

A tool re-applies a new budget rule to every shipped level and refuses to write anything if any level's tier would move. A separate test guarantees that spending the entire budget is always one star, so the budget can never be cut so far that a win scores nothing.

## Drawing the curve

With a way to make and measure boards, the last step is choosing 100 of them for each pack, in order.

The first attempt sorted boards into tier blocks: all the Easy ones, then all the Medium ones, and so on. Playing it showed the problem at once. Levels 1 to 20 were all easy, twelve of them the same four-jar, two-spice shape, and difficulty came in plateaus.

So the curve is now **drawn, not sorted**:

1. Every candidate board gets a **difficulty score** from its tier, its route length and its traps.
2. We draw the curve we want: six teaching levels growing from 4 to 7 jars, nothing below Medium after that, and irregular spikes every two to four levels with a breather after each.
3. Each slot takes the unused board whose score is **nearest** to the curve's value there, within a tolerance.
4. If no board is close enough, assembly **fails loudly** instead of forcing a board into a slot it did not earn.

![Diagram: building the curve. A pool of measured boards, each with a difficulty score, is matched slot by slot to a drawn target curve with spikes and breathers. Each slot takes the nearest unused board within a tolerance; if none fits, assembly fails loudly rather than forcing one.](/blog/spicecraft/02-drawn-curve.svg)

The mechanics also arrive along the curve: jars of different sizes first appear at level 7, ceramic jars at level 8, and the masala bowl at level 14.

Building a pool first and then filling the curve was itself a lesson. The earlier approach, "keep generating until you get a board of this tier", loops quietly and tells you nothing when it struggles. A pool shows you exactly what you have and what is missing. In the first pack's pool of 2,905 boards, for example, only 66 were Hard, against 985 Xhard. The scarce tier was not the hardest one, and the pool made that obvious.

### One rule we deliberately did not use

Puzzle design advice often says every level should have exactly one solution. That is a property of deduction puzzles, like sudoku. A sort puzzle is a rearrangement puzzle: independent pours can be played in almost any order, so every solvable board has an enormous number of solution paths. Requiring a unique solution would reject every board ever generated.

## Reproducible, and fast enough

Every candidate board comes from a seed built from the pack's seed, the bucket it belongs to and its position in that bucket. The pack's seed is written into the level file. Running the same generation with the same seed produces a **byte-for-byte identical** file, and a test checks exactly that. New kinds of boards are appended after the existing ones, so adding them never re-rolls a board that already shipped.

Measuring thousands of candidates is slow, so it runs on every processor core at once, one solver per core, with results gathered back in their original order. A test checks that the multi-core result is identical to the single-core one.

The speed-up taught us something. The first pack's pool took 920 seconds on one core and 276 seconds on fourteen: only 3.3 times faster, not fourteen. The floor is the slowest single board, and no number of cores makes one board faster. For the second pack, five cores (587 seconds) were nearly as fast as fourteen (607 seconds), so five is the default. Measuring it first is why generation still runs on a laptop's cores rather than on a rented cloud machine.

## The second hundred

Levels 101 to 200 came from a second generation run with its own seed and a stricter recipe:

- Its mix of tiers is exact: 10 Medium, 40 Medium-hard, 28 Hard and 22 Xhard.
- On Medium and Medium-hard boards, at most one in three opening pours may be a trap.
- It rejects any board that repeats one from the first pack, including recoloured or reordered versions of the same board.

The first pack did not hit its target mix exactly (it landed close: 4 Easy, 2 Easy-medium, 24 Medium, 40 Medium-hard, 14 Hard and 16 Xhard), and we record it as it is rather than as it was planned.

## What runs on the phone

Generation stays offline. During play, the phone runs only a few small searches, each with a fixed budget: one to notice when a board has become impossible to win, one to find a hint, and one behind the "room for mistakes" ring. All three share the same search code as the generator. As the hint code's comment puts it, "two copies would drift".

Before allowing a search on a phone at all, we measured it against every board a player could reach across all 200 levels: 28,031 positions. The worst needed 3,666 nodes, against a budget of 200,000. The median took 0.006 milliseconds, and 99.9% finished within 0.95 milliseconds. It never once ran out of budget.

Two lessons came out of measuring that properly:

- **Sample everything, not the easy part.** A first measurement that only sampled positions near the start reported a worst case of 1,402 nodes. The real worst case was 3,666.
- **Check what a slow number is.** An early "2.48 millisecond" maximum turned out to be a garbage-collection pause, not the search.

That measurement is now a test, run across every shipped level.

## The guarantees, and the tests that hold them

Claims like "every level can be finished" are only worth something if a test fails when they stop being true. These are some of the checks that run against the shipped level files:

- Every level is solvable, and its par is the **re-computed** proven minimum plus two.
- Playing a level's shortest route wins it in exactly its proven minimum number of moves.
- Every level gives the minimum some room, and a budget to spend it from.
- A player who does **nothing but follow hints**, on every single move, wins all 200 levels inside their budgets. On average they use 70% of the budget, and their routes are 1.07 times the shortest.

That last one deserves a sentence of explanation. A hint is only ever a pour from a route that fits in the moves you have left. After you play it, the rest of that route still fits in one fewer move. Repeat that, and following hints can never lose. The test simply checks the reasoning on every level.

## In numbers

| | Levels 1 to 100 | Levels 101 to 200 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vessels per level (including the bowl) | 4 to 9 | 5 to 10 |
| Spices per level | 2 to 7 | 4 to 8 |
| Proven minimum moves | 7 to 26 (median 17) | 11 to 31 (median 19) |
| Move budgets | 11 to 47 | 16 to 43 |
| Levels with ceramic jars | 45 | 66 |
| Levels with a masala bowl | 28 | 34 |

## What we learned

1. **If you cannot prove it, do not ship it.** One estimated minimum of 84 against a real 24 is enough to make the rule obvious.
2. **Decide carefully what "the same position" means.** It is the easiest place for a solver to be confidently wrong.
3. **Measure difficulty by playing, not by counting.** Colours and jars are bookkeeping; robots that play tell you what a person will feel.
4. **Build a pool, then draw the curve.** You see what you have, and assembly can refuse instead of forcing a bad fit.
5. **Make it reproducible.** One seed, one byte-identical file, and new boards that never disturb old ones.
6. **Measure the whole space before trusting a number on a phone.** The easy part of the space will flatter you.

SpiceCraft is free on [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.spicecraft), and the iPhone version is coming soon.

Previously in this series: [why our first game is a sort puzzle](/blog/why-our-first-game-is-a-sort-puzzle). Next: [room for mistakes](/blog/spicecraft-room-for-mistakes-move-budget-and-hints), on the move budget, stars and a hint that always leads to a win.

title: Room for mistakes: designing a fair move budget, honest feedback and a hint that cannot lose
excerpt: How SpiceCraft tells a player how much slack they have left without ever lying: the move budget, the 'room for mistakes' ring that only moves on proof, the bug where it said 83% on a lost board, star rules, optional helpers and a hint that provably cannot lose.
content:
Every SpiceCraft level gives you a number of moves. Spend them well and you win. Waste too many and you run out.

That raises a design question we spent more time on than almost anything else in the game: **how do you tell a player how they are doing, without lying to them, and without solving the puzzle for them?**

This post is about that question. It covers the move budget, the "room for mistakes" ring above the board, the two different ways a level can be lost, how stars are awarded, the optional helpers behind short videos, and a hint that is mathematically unable to lead you to a loss. It also covers the day our ring said **83%** on a board that was already lost, and what we changed because of it. It is part three of our series on building SpiceCraft.

### A short glossary

- **Move budget:** how many pours a level gives you.
- **Minimum:** the fewest pours that can win the level, proven by a solver before the level ships. Our [previous post](/blog/spicecraft-200-levels-every-one-solvable) explains how.
- **Par:** the minimum plus 2. Finish at or under par for three stars.
- **Room:** how many spare moves you have beyond what the board still needs.
- **Rewarded video:** a short ad a player chooses to watch in exchange for help, such as a hint.
- **Interstitial:** a full-screen ad shown between levels, which the player did not choose.
- **Proof:** here, an answer from a complete search, as opposed to a guess or an estimate.

## A move budget, never a timer

SpiceCraft has no timers. Nothing ticks down while you think. The only pressure is the number of moves, and the budget is set from the proven minimum: par times 1.25, plus two extra moves for every ceramic jar (finding hidden spice costs pours) and two for every slot in a recipe bowl.

The moves counter changes colour as it runs low: **amber at 3 moves left, red and pulsing at 1.** Those thresholds were 5 and 2 at first. Then we noticed that on 13 levels the counter turned amber even if you played the **perfect** route, which is a warning about nothing. At 3, the shortest route never sees amber.

Undo exists, and it gives the move back. You get two undos per level, and none on the two hardest tiers.

## Two ways to lose, and why they get different answers

A level can end badly in two very different ways, and treating them the same would be both unhelpful and unfair.

![Diagram: two ways a level can be lost. Out of moves is about the budget: the board can still be won, so the offer is five more moves, once per attempt. Stuck is about the board: no number of moves can win it, so the offers change the board instead: a spare jar, undo when it can reach a winnable board, or restart.](/blog/spicecraft/03-two-ways-to-fail.svg)

**Out of moves** is about the budget. The board might still be winnable; you just spent everything. So the answer is more moves: a short video for five extra moves, offered **once per attempt**. If you run out again, the sheet offers a restart or a way home, and nothing else.

There used to be a paid version of that button, at $0.99. We removed it, because there was no working purchase behind it. The comment in the code says it in one line: "A button that lies is worse than no button."

**Stuck** is about the board. Either there is no legal pour at all, or there are legal pours but the board has been **proven** impossible to win. More moves cannot fix that, so the Stuck sheet offers ways to change the board instead: one spare jar, undo (only when undoing can actually reach a winnable board), restart, or home.

### Letting a trap bite

There is one deliberate delay in all this. When a board becomes unwinnable but you still have legal pours, the Stuck sheet waits **three more pours** before it appears. We call this "let the trap bite, then rescue".

The reason is learning. If the game announced a trap the instant you sprang it, you would never feel the moment of "oh, that was the mistake". The delay is the game's cruelty dial, and three pours is where we set it. When there are no legal pours at all, there is nothing to learn from waiting, and the sheet appears at once.

## The ring: how much room do you have left?

Above the board sits a small brass ring with a percentage in it. Its job is to answer one question while you play: **how much room for mistakes do I still have?**

### It started as the wrong number

The ring first shipped as a "chance to win from here". On some levels it opened at 15 to 27%, before the player had done anything. Our own reaction when we saw it on a phone was the obvious one: "I expect 100% at the start of every game."

We could have tried to make the estimate smarter. Instead, we noticed the problem was the **meaning**. Even with a perfect search, a "win chance" formula would have opened at 100% on only 9 of the 200 levels. So we changed what the ring measures.

### What it measures now

**Room** is the moves you have left, minus the fewest pours the board still needs. The ring shows that room as a share of the room you started with:

```text
percent = round(100 × (movesLeft − stillNeeded) ÷ startRoom), kept between 0 and 100
startRoom = budget − proven minimum
```

![Diagram: how the room for mistakes ring is computed. A level with a 20-move budget and a proven minimum of 10 starts with 10 moves of room, shown as 100%. After four pours, one of them wasted, there are 16 moves left and the board still needs at least 7, so the room is 9 and the ring reads 90%.](/blog/spicecraft/03-room-formula.svg)

Because every level's minimum is proven exactly, every level opens at **exactly 100%**, before any search runs. One wasted pour costs one "notch": one move's share of the starting room. Across our levels the starting room runs from 4 moves to 23, so a notch is anywhere from 25% to about 4%.

Two small rules keep the extremes honest. 0% and 100% each mean exactly one thing: a sliver of room never rounds down to 0, and a ring that is not quite full never rounds up to 100.

### The ring only moves on proof

"The fewest pours the board still needs" is not something the game knows for free. After every pour, it has to work it out again. That happens in the background, so the game never stutters, and it follows one rule above all others: **the ring moves only on proof.**

- To **drop**, the game needs proof that the board needs more pours than before.
- To **rise**, it needs a route it has actually found.
- If a search is unsure (it ran out of budget), the ring **holds**.

Most of the time, no search is needed at all. The game keeps the route it last found; if your pour was on that route, the route still works and nothing changes. When a search is needed, it is a short, targeted question ("is there a route of at most this many pours?"), with a fixed budget so it can never slow the phone down.

We measured how well this works by having simulated players make hundreds of thousands of pours:

| | Perfect player | Imperfect player |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Good pours that wrongly lowered the ring | **0 of 46,020** | 0.15%, each by a single notch |
| Wasted pours not shown straight away | none to show | 1.5% |
| Searches needed for a typical pour | none | none |

The ring is not perfect, and we do not claim it is. It sometimes takes a little while to notice a wasted pour, and for an imperfect player it very occasionally lowers a notch too early. But for a perfect player, it never once blamed a good pour.

One more honest detail. The searches behind the ring see the true contents of ceramic jars, not just what you have uncovered. So the ring leaks a tiny amount of information about hidden spice. We considered a ring that only knows what you can see, and chose not to build it. We accepted the small leak instead, and wrote down that we had.

The ring also stays brass at all times. It never flashes or changes colour; a change is a quiet 150 ms sweep with no sound. The moves counter is the alarm. The ring is information.

## The day it said 83%

On 20 October 2026, while testing on a phone, we hit this on level 81: the ring read **83% room for mistakes**, and in the same moment the Hint button said **"No way to win from here."**

Both cannot be true. Our first thought was a calculation bug. It was not. It was a **design contradiction**, and the code was doing exactly what two different rules told it to do.

- The ring followed the "let the trap bite" rule from the Stuck sheet. On a losing pour it dropped one notch per pour, and only reached 0% when the Stuck sheet appeared three pours later.
- The Hint followed its own rule: on a board proven lost, refuse at once, for free, and say why.

Both parts of the game knew the board was lost from the fourth pour. The solver had proven it, in 12 positions, as the jar landed. One part told the truth straight away. The other told what we called, in the bug report, "a white lie": 94%, then 89%, then 83%, while the real room was zero.

Digging further turned up two more problems hiding in the same place:

- **The hint was already giving every trap away for free.** So the ring's polite delay protected nothing.
- **The Stuck sheet's Undo could never get back to before the losing pour.** The sheet waited three pours, but you only have two undos. So "undo or restart" was, at best, half true.

### The fix: one board, one reading

We wrote down what "correct" means for this ring: **never contradict the game, and never blame a good pour.** Then we changed three things:

1. **A lost board reads 0% the moment it is proven lost**, with the caption "no way to win". The Stuck sheet still waits its three pours, so the trap still bites. But the ring no longer pretends.
2. **One shared reading per board.** The stuck check, the ring and the hint now all feed one shared record of what is known about the current board, and all read from it. They cannot disagree, because there is only one answer to disagree about.
3. **"Undo" is only offered when undo can reach a winnable board**, on both the hint's message and the Stuck sheet.

![Diagram: one shared reading per board. The stuck check, the ring's search and the hint all write what they prove into one shared reading of the current board, and all three read from it, so the ring, the hint and the Stuck sheet always say the same thing.](/blog/spicecraft/03-one-reading.svg)

The same change fixed a second contradiction nobody had reported yet: the hint saying "not enough moves left to win" while the ring still showed room. The ring now has three captions, and each one needs a proof: "room for mistakes" while the board is alive, "not enough moves" when it is proven short, and "no way to win" when it is proven lost.

The review of that fix found two more edge cases (a board with a spare jar that could be saved as lost, and a saved loss that was trusted without being proven again), plus a race between a question already in flight and a new answer from the hint. All three were fixed before release. The flagship test now plays level 81 itself and checks that the ring, the hint and the Stuck sheet say "lost" together.

The test suite for this part of the game was checked the hard way: we broke 24 of its safeguards on purpose, one at a time. The tests caught 23. The 24th guarded code that was then removed.

## Stars

Stars are the game's long-term feedback, and they follow simple rules:

- **Three stars:** finish at or under par (the minimum plus 2).
- **Two stars:** finish under par times 1.2.
- **One star:** any other win.

The two-star line used to be par times 1.4. When budgets were tightened (see our previous post), that old line became impossible to reach on 60 of the first 100 levels. So it moved to 1.2. A test makes sure that spending your **entire** budget is always one star, at every par, so a tighter budget can never make a hard-won finish worthless.

### Help caps a win at two stars

Since late September, using any paid help (a peek, a hint, the spare jar or the five extra moves) caps that win at two stars. Undo does not count, because it is free and limited.

We were careful to record the honest reason for this rule. It was not that the helpers make levels easy: we measured the spare jar, and on 7 of 8 levels it saved **zero** moves. It is insurance, not a shortcut. The real reason is consistency. Without the cap, a win card could show three gold stars next to a message about needing help, and the two would contradict each other.

We also recorded the cost honestly: rewarded videos pay for the game, and this rule could make players less willing to watch them. We do not yet have the data to know. A three-star score you have already earned is never lowered by a later replay that used help.

### What the game says when you win

The win card picks its line from what actually happened. A perfect route with no help gets lines like "Flawless!" or **"No grain wasted"**. Winning with one move to spare gets "Close call!". Winning after the five extra moves gets "Pulled it back!". Winning a ceramic level without ever peeking has its own line too.

## The hint that cannot lose

The hint shows you one pour. It costs one short video, and you can use at most three per attempt.

It has one unusual property: **the pour is found before the video is offered.** If there is no useful pour to give (the board is lost, or there are not enough moves left), you are told why, in plain words, and no video plays and nothing is spent:

- "No way to win from here - undo or restart" (and it only mentions undo when undo can actually help)
- "Not enough moves left to win"
- "No hint right now - nothing spent", if the search gave up

Selling a hint and then discovering there is nothing to give would be the worst kind of ad. So the search runs first, for free.

### Why following hints can never lose

A hint is always the first pour of a route that **fits in the moves you have left**. After you play it, the rest of that route fits in one fewer move. Ask again, and the same is true. By induction, a player who follows hints all the way will always win.

We do not just reason about this; we test it. One test plays every one of the 200 levels using nothing but hints, one per move. It wins all of them, using 70% of the budget on average, with routes 1.07 times the length of the shortest. The test fails if that ratio ever reaches 1.2.

The hint deliberately does **not** insist on the shortest possible pour. When it tried to, it gave up on 7.25% of Medium boards within its budget. "First route that fits, then shorten it a little" gives up on none.

One last guard: the board is still live while the video plays. If the board changed in the meantime, the hint is not shown on a board it was not found for. The message reads "The board moved on - that hint is still yours."

## The optional helpers

Every helper in SpiceCraft is a rewarded video. Each is only granted if the video finishes; otherwise the game says "No ad available - nothing spent".

| Helper | What it does | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Peek** | Reveals the top hidden layer of the ceramic jar hiding the most | Until nothing is hidden; one video per layer |
| **Spare jar** | Adds one empty jar to the shelf. It is a purchase, not a move, so undo never takes it away | Once per level |
| **Five more moves** | Continues after the budget runs out | Once per attempt |
| **Hint** | Shows one pour from a winning route | Three per attempt |

None of them is ever required. Every level has been solved by a program inside its budget, and the free ways out of a bad position are undo and restart.

A finding from early design shaped this table: **an unlimited offer is almost never right in this genre.** The spare jar was once unlimited. Pressing it repeatedly made the shelf shrink until the game was unplayable, and, worse, it stopped the level being a puzzle at all. The thing being offered is the scarce resource the puzzle is built on.

### A nudge that is free

There is also one piece of help that costs nothing. If you tap three pours in a row that are not allowed, the two jars of some legal pour gently "breathe". It says "this pour is **possible**", not "this pour is **good**", and following it can lower your ring.

## When the full-screen ads appear

SpiceCraft also shows a full-screen ad roughly every fourth level, and we spent as much care on **when not to show one**:

- The count is of finished levels and restarts that threw away real progress, not of level numbers.
- No full-screen ad within **90 seconds** of another one closing. The case that prompted this was a player who watched a video for five more moves, won, and got another ad seconds later.
- Never from the Out of moves sheet. That player has just declined a video; another ad at the most frustrating moment of the game would be unkind.
- Never for a restart where you had done nothing.
- If you watched a video during the level, it replaces the full-screen ad that level would have earned.

Each of those rules has its own test.

## What we learned

1. **Decide what a number means before improving how it is calculated.** A smarter "win chance" would still have opened at 15%. Changing the meaning fixed it.
2. **Two honest rules can add up to a lie.** The ring and the hint were each correct alone. Shared state, not a better formula, was the fix.
3. **Move only on proof, hold when unsure.** A feedback signal that sometimes stays still is far better than one that sometimes accuses you wrongly.
4. **Find the reward before you sell it.** A hint that might be empty must not cost a video.
5. **Write down the honest reason, and the honest cost.** The star cap is about consistency, not difficulty, and we do not know yet what it costs us.
6. **Break your safeguards on purpose.** A test that has never failed has not been tested.

SpiceCraft is free on [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.spicecraft), and the iPhone version is coming soon. Level 81 is in there, if you would like to see the board that taught us all this.

More in this series: [why our first game is a sort puzzle](/blog/why-our-first-game-is-a-sort-puzzle) and [how all 200 levels are proven solvable](/blog/spicecraft-200-levels-every-one-solvable).

title: The prototype is the specification: building SpiceCraft in a browser first, then porting it to Unity
excerpt: Before writing any Unity code, we built SpiceCraft as one HTML file and tuned every colour, timing and curve there. How that prototype became the specification, what it caught that code review never would, and how the port kept the rules testable without Unity.
content:
Before we wrote a single line of Unity code for SpiceCraft, the whole game already existed. It was one HTML file: about 1,200 lines of plain JavaScript, hand-drawn SVG art and a small particle system, with no framework, no build step and no dependencies. You could open it in a browser and play.

That file answered the two questions that are most expensive to get wrong in a game, before any expensive work started: **does the loop feel good, and does the theme look right?**

Then it became something more unusual. We made it the **specification**. Every colour, every animation timing and every easing curve in the shipped Unity game was read out of that file, not written from memory or from a design document.

This post explains why we worked that way, what the prototype caught that reading code never did, how we ported it without porting its mess, and the one rule that stopped the prototype from becoming a trap. It is part four of our series on building SpiceCraft.

### A short glossary

- **Prototype:** a quick, rough version of a product built to answer questions, not to ship.
- **Port:** rebuilding something on a different platform. Here, from a web page to the Unity game engine.
- **Easing curve:** how an animation speeds up and slows down. A ball that slows as it lands "eases out".
- **Tween:** a short animation from one value to another, such as moving a jar from one place to another over 200 milliseconds.
- **DOTween:** a popular Unity library for writing tweens in code.
- **Play Mode:** running the game inside the Unity editor, as opposed to just editing it.
- **Simulator:** a virtual iPhone running on a Mac, used for testing without a physical phone.

## Why a browser prototype, for a Unity game

Unity is a powerful engine, and it is slow to iterate in for the questions we cared about first. Every change means a compile, a domain reload, and often a click through the editor. A web page reloads in a second.

The first questions were all about feel:

- How high should a jar lift before it moves sideways?
- How long should a pour take?
- When a jar is finished, when should its lid land?
- Which colours can a player tell apart at a glance?

None of these can be answered by thinking. They can only be answered by trying a value, watching it, and trying another. A browser is the fastest place in the world to do that.

The prototype was also deliberately ugly on the inside. One file, global state, art built by gluing strings together. That is the right shape for answering design questions fast, and the wrong shape for a shipped game. We wrote that down on day one, so nobody would try to copy its architecture later.

## The values are the deliverable

Here is the idea that made the prototype worth more than a sketch: **the numbers it produced were the product.**

Planning cannot tell you that a jar must lift exactly high enough to clear the tallest jar in the row. Tuning can. So we treated every tuned value as a deliverable, and wrote a mapping document from each prototype value to its place in Unity.

The pour is the best example. It happens hundreds of times in a session, so it has to feel right. In the prototype it is five steps on the travelling jar:

| Step | What the jar does | How long |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Lifts straight up | 200 ms |
| 2 | Travels across and tips toward the target | 235 ms |
| 3 | Holds while it empties | 150 ms plus 75 ms per unit poured |
| 4 | Rises and turns upright again | 250 ms |
| 5 | Drops back home, with a small overshoot | 260 ms |

Each step also has its own easing curve, written as exact numbers. In the prototype, the function that runs the pour was written as a plain list of steps on purpose, so that in Unity it maps one to one onto a DOTween sequence: five `Append` calls, one per step.

![Diagram: the SpiceCraft prototype, one HTML file, hands its tuned values to the Unity game. The rules go into a pure C# library tested without Unity; the look and motion go into a presentation layer tested in Play Mode and on the simulator. A dashed arrow says evidence can overrule the prototype.](/blog/spicecraft/04-prototype-to-unity.svg)

Other details came out the same way:

- **In the prototype, a finished jar's lid landed 300 ms late, on purpose.** The lid is the full stop. It should land after the last band of spice has finished filling, not on top of it.
- **Spice grains fly from the jar's measured lip, every frame.** More on why below.
- **Each prototype pour threw between 26 and 90 grains**, so in the game the grains are pooled (reused) rather than created and destroyed every time.
- **The colours are ordered by how different each is from the ones before it**, not by hue. Early levels only use the first few colours, and ordering by hue dealt three similar warm tones into level one.

## What the prototype caught that reading code never did

This is the strongest argument for the whole approach, so we kept a list. Five real bugs were found in the prototype, and **not one of them was found by reading the source**:

1. **The travelling jar flew through the row instead of over it.** The lift was shorter than the jar's own height. Found by watching a screen recording.
2. **The jar clipped a neighbour on its way back.** It came down diagonally while still over the next jar. Found by measuring the overlap between elements every 50 milliseconds.
3. **The stream of spice detached from the jar** and floated in mid-air. The grains came from a fixed point instead of the jar's real lip. Found in the same recording.
4. **A five-unit spice filled a four-unit jar, looked finished, and locked itself**, leaving the board quietly impossible to win. Found by playing.
5. **The board shrank to a hairline** when the extra-jar button was pressed over and over. Found by playing.

Every one of these was invisible in the code and obvious on screen. That changed how we define "done". A change that compiles and reads well is not accepted. A change is accepted when it has been **seen working**.

### Two rules that look like style, but are bug fixes

Bugs 1 and 2 became permanent rules for the pour:

1. **The lift must be higher than the tallest jar.** The prototype lifted 160 px against a tallest jar of 146 px. In Unity this is not hard-coded: it is computed from the tallest jar on the board plus a clearance, so the rule survives any change to the jar art.
2. **The rise and the return must be perfectly vertical at their ends.** Any sideways drift while the jar is still at row height clips its neighbour.

We checked the fix the same way we found the bug: by measuring the travelling jar against every other jar at 50 ms intervals through the whole animation. Zero overlap across 23 samples. A diagonal path looks smoother, and it is broken. Our notes say, in bold: do not "improve" it.

## Porting the values, not the mess

The Unity version does not copy the prototype's structure. It copies its **numbers** and its **rules**, into a structure built for a game that has to be maintained.

### The rules live in a library that cannot see Unity

The most important decision in the Unity project is a split into two parts:

- **Core:** the rules of the game. Boards, jars, what counts as a legal pour, what counts as finished, the recipe bowl, and the level generator. It is pure C#, and Unity is told explicitly that this part may not reference the engine at all.
- **Game:** everything the player sees and touches. Jars, the pour animation, sounds, menus and ads.

Keeping the rules away from the engine means they can be tested with plain `dotnet test`, on a machine with no Unity installed, in seconds. That matters because a bug in the rules is invisible until a player meets an impossible board, and by then it is too late.

### Every feel value lives in one editable place

Every duration, easing curve and colour in the Game layer lives in a settings file the team can edit in Unity's editor (a ScriptableObject). Tuning how a pour feels is a change to a number, not a code change, and each value says which prototype function it came from.

### A latent bug the port planning found

Writing down the mapping carefully caught one more problem, this time in the prototype's level checker.

To avoid exploring the same position twice, the prototype's search identified a board by **sorting all the jars' contents together**. That was correct when every jar was the same. It stopped being correct the moment jars came in different sizes and kinds. Swapping the contents of a three-unit jar and a five-unit jar gives a genuinely different position, but the old key said they were the same. A glass jar and a ceramic jar of the same size are not interchangeable either, because one hides what is inside.

It had never been seen producing a bad level. It might have been hidden by the generator simply reshuffling past any board it rejected. But it was the riskiest piece of logic in the project, and fixing it was cheap in a fresh implementation and expensive to retrofit. So the Unity version **sorts jars only within groups of the same size and kind**, and that rule is now part of the solver's written contract. [Part two of this series](/blog/spicecraft-200-levels-every-one-solvable) goes into the solver in depth.

## The prototype is a strong default, not a trump card

After a few weeks, we hit the obvious problem with "the prototype is the specification". What if the prototype is wrong?

So we added a rule: **evidence beats the prototype.** A measurement, a playtest or published research can overrule a prototype value. Preference cannot. And when a value is overruled, the reason is written next to the value, with the evidence.

Two real examples:

**The pour got faster, then too fast, then right.** The first Unity build took its pour timings from a later design mock-up, about 2.15 seconds for a one-unit pour. In the game, a pour blocks input, and two seconds per move is the biggest risk to how a tap-tap-watch game feels. So it was cut back to the web prototype's 1.2 seconds. Two days later, after measuring a reference recording frame by frame, it was cut again to about 0.83 seconds, with your next tap accepted as soon as the jar starts to right itself. That same evening, playing it on a phone, it felt rushed, and a jar pouring down to a lower row hung a whole row-height above its target. So the jar now dips toward the target's own mouth, and a one-unit pour takes about 1.09 seconds, with your next tap accepted from about 0.63 seconds in. Every one of those changes is written next to the value, with its reason, in the one file that holds the timings.

**Hidden spice changed colour.** In ceramic jars, spice you cannot see yet is drawn as a hatched placeholder. The design file painted it in a dark green that turned out to be, byte for byte, the ceramic jar's own shadow colour. So a ceramic jar full of unknown spice looked just like an **empty** ceramic jar. Which jars are empty is the single most important thing a sort puzzle asks a player to read. A player found it on level 62. We measured the two on the simulator at a colour difference of 15.1, below the minimum the game allows between any two spices, and switched the placeholder to a warm grey, measured at 20.7 afterwards. A test now enforces the rule behind the fix: hidden spice may never be painted in any colour the jar itself uses.

The second example is the pattern we like most. The fix is a number, the reason is a measurement, and the rule is a test.

## Testing a game the way a player meets it

The prototype taught us that the screen is where bugs show up. The Unity port taught us a harder lesson: **the editor is not far enough, for anything a finger touches.**

Three more bugs turned up only on a phone. Empty jars had their tap area switched off. The board rebuilt itself blank when the iPhone's safe area (the space around the notch) arrived. The whole layout was sized for a wider screen shape than modern phones have.

The first one is the one we tell people about. Our automated player, which plays levels to check they can be won, **passed the entire time.** It played by calling the game's tap handler directly. It never went through the real touch system, so it could not see that the empty jars could not be tapped. Every board that needed an empty jar as a destination was impossible to win on a real phone, and the automated check said all was well.

The lesson we wrote down: **an automated check that reaches past the layer where the bug lives will pass a broken game, and do it convincingly.**

So SpiceCraft has three test harnesses, and which one a test goes in depends on what it can prove:

| Harness | Runs on | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core tests | Plain `dotnet test`, no Unity | Rules, solver and level generation. Seconds |
| Edit Mode tests | Unity, without playing | Facts about the project: scenes and references are wired up |
| Play Mode tests | Unity, playing, with real frames | The game layer, through the real touch raycast |

And on top of the tests, for anything a player touches, a final step: build the game, install it on the iPhone simulator and tap it. A single command does the export, compile, install and launch in about 45 seconds, and a small script sends real taps. (A tap has to be held for about a quarter of a second, or the simulator does not count it as one, which was its own afternoon of confusion.)

### A test has to be seen failing

One more habit came out of this. A test that has never been seen to fail is not verified. So when we write a test for a bug, we put the bug back on purpose, watch the test go red, then remove it again.

That has already caught weak tests that passed while proving nothing. One example: an early attempt to revive the "untappable empty jar" bug changed a value that the game overwrote a few microseconds later. The test stayed green, and for a moment looked worthless. The test was fine; the mutation was in the wrong layer. **A mutation only counts if it breaks the layer the bug actually lived on.**

## What we would do again

1. **Prototype feel where iteration is cheapest.** For us that was a single HTML file. The engine came later.
2. **Treat the tuned numbers as the deliverable**, and map each one to its new home when you port.
3. **Do not port the prototype's architecture.** Port its values and its rules into a structure built for maintenance.
4. **Keep the rules in a library that cannot see the engine**, so they can be tested in seconds anywhere.
5. **Let evidence overrule the prototype, and write the evidence down** next to the value it changed.
6. **Test through the layer the player uses.** For a game, that means a real tap on a real (or simulated) screen.

The prototype is still in the repository, and we still open it beside the game when something feels off. Comparing the two side by side catches things no review can.

SpiceCraft is free on [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.spicecraft), and the iPhone version is coming soon.

Earlier in this series: [why our first game is a sort puzzle](/blog/why-our-first-game-is-a-sort-puzzle) and [how all 200 levels are proven solvable](/blog/spicecraft-200-levels-every-one-solvable).
