title: Game feel by measurement: colours you can tell apart, the sound of a pour, and why we shipped without haptics
excerpt: How SpiceCraft turns game feel into numbers it can test: a spice palette held to a perceptual colour-difference floor, a room drawn with zero image files, a sound mix pinned by tests, and the honest reason the first version has no vibration.
content:
"Game feel" usually gets described in words like *juicy*, *satisfying* and *polished*. Those words are real, but you cannot test them. A pull request that says "made it feel better" cannot fail.

For SpiceCraft we tried to turn as much of game feel as we could into **numbers**: numbers we could measure on a real screen, write into a test, and refuse to break. This post covers four parts of that: the colours, the room the jars sit in, the sound, and the one part of feel we chose **not** to ship, vibration. It is the last part of our five-part series on building SpiceCraft.

### A short glossary

- **Colour difference (ΔE, "delta E"):** a number for how different two colours look to a person. Around 1 is barely noticeable; bigger is easier to tell apart.
- **CIEDE2000 and CIE76:** two standard formulas for colour difference. CIE76 is older and simpler; CIEDE2000 is a correction that matches human eyes much better, especially for blues.
- **dBFS:** decibels relative to "full scale", the loudest a digital audio file can be. 0 is the maximum; -20 is much quieter.
- **Ducking:** turning the music down so something else can be heard.
- **Haptics:** small, precise vibrations a phone uses to make a tap or event feel physical.
- **Frame time:** how long the phone takes to draw one picture. 16.7 milliseconds per frame is 60 frames a second.

## Colours a player can tell apart

In a sort puzzle, colour **is** the game. If two spices look alike, the puzzle becomes unfair in a way no amount of skill can fix. So the palette was the first part of game feel we measured.

### Eight spices, in a deliberate order

SpiceCraft uses eight spice colours: saffron, crimson, jade, cobalt, ember, violet, teal and pepper. Each has three shades: a main colour that is the spice's identity (the one a player would name it by), a lighter strip along the top of each layer, and a darker one at its base.

The order matters more than it looks. Early levels only use the first few spices. If the list were sorted by hue, level one would deal three neighbouring warm tones, and they are genuinely hard to read at a glance. So the list is ordered by **how different each spice is from the ones before it**. Whatever number of spices a level uses, it gets the most distinct set available.

We also learned that cool colours are not optional in a warm, spice-themed game. Without a true blue, a violet and a teal, the set collapses into what our notes call "warm mud".

![Diagram: SpiceCraft's eight spice colours in their dealing order, saffron, crimson, jade, cobalt, ember, violet, teal and pepper, with the rule that every pair must be at least 15 apart on the CIEDE2000 colour-difference scale. The closest pair, cobalt and violet, measures 15.7.](/blog/spicecraft/05-palette-floor.svg)

### Measuring with the right formula

To hold the palette to a standard, we measure the difference between every pair of spice colours. We started with the classic CIE76 formula, and it misled us in two ways.

1. **It overstates differences between saturated blues and violets**, which happen to be our cobalt and our violet. CIE76 scored that pair 30.8, comfortably apart. CIEDE2000, which tracks human vision more closely, scores it **15.7**: our closest pair, not one of our safest.
2. **It reorders the palette.** CIE76 ranked jade against teal as only the fourth-closest pair, at 53. Perceptually it is the **second**-closest, at 21.7.

A formula that gets the order wrong tells you to worry about the wrong colours. So the game now measures with CIEDE2000, and the old formula is kept only to check older recorded figures.

### A floor, enforced twice

The rule is simple: **no two spices may be less than 15 apart.** The closest pair is 15.7, so the floor locks in the legibility the game already has, and stops any future change from eroding it.

It is enforced in two places:

- **At runtime.** If a colour settings file ever fails the check, the game refuses it and falls back to its built-in colours. A bad edit cannot ship an unreadable palette.
- **In a test.** And the test spells out the number 15 directly, rather than reading it from the code. That sounds pedantic until you hear why: we once checked the test by setting the floor to a third of its value on purpose, and the whole test file still passed, because the test read the floor from the same code it was meant to be checking. Writing the literal number in the test fixed that.

### Measuring everything that sits next to a spice

Spices are not only seen next to each other. They sit inside jars, under selection rings, in the recipe bowl and against the room. So the same kind of measurement is applied to all of those, and almost every one has a story.

**The jar that looked empty.** Ceramic jars hide the spice below the top layer, drawn as a hatched placeholder. During playtesting on level 62, the ceramic jars caught our eye, and measuring them found the bug: a ceramic jar full of hidden spice and an **empty** ceramic jar looked almost the same. The placeholder had been painted in a dark green that was, byte for byte, the ceramic jar's own shadow colour. Measured on the simulator, a full and an empty ceramic jar were just 15.1 apart, below the floor we allow between two spices, when "which jars are empty" is the single most important thing a sort puzzle asks a player to read. The placeholder became a warm grey with diagonal hatching, measured at 20.7 afterwards.

That fix taught a second lesson. The first test compared the two **assigned** colours, which were 20.2 apart. But on screen they are drawn on top of each other with transparency, and the **composited** result was what closed the gap to 15.1. The first test passed with the bug put back in. The real test measures what is actually drawn, and uses a stricter floor of 20, because the looser 15 let a pale sage through at 15.96.

**The ring you could not see on saffron.** A brass highlight ring, drawn over saffron's lighter strip, measured just 5.3 apart. Saffron appears in all 200 levels. The ring gained a dark inner edge, and the worst case became 29.2.

**The bowl that swallowed saffron.** The masala recipe bowl was brass. Saffron poured into it measured 12.5 against the bowl's inside, below the floor every pair of spices must clear. On a phone, saffron nearly disappeared. We compared four materials, and the bowl became marble. On marble, the weakest spice (saffron again) measures 24.7. The trade was written down before the choice: marble is the brightest thing on the screen.

**The cork that carries "finished".** A completed jar is sealed with a cork and a run of wax. The wax measured only 7.3 against the jar's collar, too close to read. The cork measured 39.2. So the cork, not the wax, is what tells you a jar is done.

### What we have not done yet

We have not tested the palette against colour-vision deficiency simulations. The game uses more than colour to separate some states (the selected jar lifts; finished jars wear a cork; hidden layers are hatched), but we do not claim the spices are colour-blind safe. It is on the list.

## A room with zero image files

The jars stand in a dark spice mill at dusk. There is no background image. The whole room is drawn in code from a few large, soft gradients: a darker wall at the top, a cool pool of light high on one side, and a warm lamp glow low on the other. Deliberately off-centre, because symmetrical shading reads as "a gradient", and asymmetrical shading reads as "a room".

An early version drew the wall as a tile grid. It read as graph paper, and it went. No repeating patterns anywhere.

Six things move, all of them cheap and reused rather than created and destroyed: the lamp breathes slowly, 24 dust motes drift, light shafts sway a couple of degrees over 9 and 12 seconds, three faint discs of haze wander, a few grains of spice sift down, and a candle flickers so slightly you mostly feel it rather than see it. Everything stops under the game's "reduce motion" setting.

### The day we found the game running at 30 frames a second

A room full of slow motion only feels smooth at a steady frame rate. In late September we discovered the game had been running at **30 frames a second** all along, because nothing had asked the phone for more. On a low-cost Android phone, every one of 125 consecutive frames took 34.0 milliseconds.

The fix was one setting to ask for 60. After it, the median frame on that same phone took 17.0 milliseconds, and the win celebration became the only moment that drops frames. We have not yet measured what the higher frame rate costs in battery, or the frame times on iPhone, and we say so in our notes rather than assuming.

## Motion that never moves at a constant speed

One rule covers every animation in the game: **never linear easing on anything that moves, scales or rotates.** Nothing in the physical world starts or stops at full speed. Entrances overshoot slightly and settle; exits ease away.

The pour is the motion players see most, so it is broken into named beats, each with its own duration and curve: rise, travel, tip, dip toward the target, untip, return, drop and settle. The hold while spice flows is 120 ms plus 60 ms per unit poured. The previous post in this series tells the story of how the pour's total time was tuned on a real phone, twice.

The win celebration is the loudest moment. Five "rockets" of grain launch from the jars 0.18 seconds apart, each bursting into a ring of 60 grains in the level's own spices, with a soft flash of the room on each burst and a rain of 80 grains to finish, three seconds in all. The win card appears **instantly**, and the celebration runs behind it, so it never makes anyone wait. Under reduce motion there are no fireworks at all, just a gentle settle.

## The sound of a pour

Sort puzzles are played with the sound on more than most casual games, and almost nobody invests in their audio. That made sound an opportunity.

### What is in the game

- **Two music tracks:** a theme for the home screen (about 1 minute 53 seconds) and a lighter bed for gameplay (46 seconds), about 3.8 MB together.
- **Thirteen recorded sound effects**, under 400 KB in total: picking up a jar, the patter of a pour, a jar completing, a cork seating, rewards and more.
- **Three sounds generated in code:** a refused pour, a failed level and a plain interface tap.

The music and eleven of the effects were generated with ElevenLabs' music and sound-effect tools, under its commercial licence. Two effects (the reward and the undo) were then built by hand from other recordings with ffmpeg, because after five attempts the generator never produced the rising pitch we asked for. The three code-generated sounds are deliberate: a refusal is the one case where sounding mechanical is correct.

There is no random pitch variation on each pour. Instead, some sounds **climb**: each jar you seal sounds slightly higher than the last, and each firework rocket in the celebration is a little higher than the one before. Progress you can hear.

### A mix that tests can hold

Loudness turned out to be the place where feel was easiest to break without noticing. So the mix is written down as numbers:

- The gameplay music sits about 9 dB below the home theme, and about 10 dB lower in the 600 Hz to 2 kHz range, where effects live, so it never fights them.
- Every effect has a target peak level, from the win sound at -5.7 dBFS down to the quiet patter of a pour at -19.9. The spread between loudest and quietest is capped at 16 dB, and a test pins the whole map.
- The files are converted to mono with ffmpeg rather than Unity's own "normalise" option, because that option would have pushed every sound to the same loudness and erased the map entirely.

The map exists because of a real bug. The "pick up a jar" sound, the most frequent sound in the game, peaked at -30.3 dBFS: about 8 dB **under** the background music. It was effectively silent. A second problem was hiding next to it: the pour patter was a three-second recording, but a pour only ever plays its first 420 milliseconds, and those were the quietest part. It is now a 500 ms recording mastered for exactly the part that is heard.

We also did a "silent state" audit: walking through every moment of the game and asking whether it should make a sound. Five silent moments got sounds. Two were left silent on purpose: the start of a level, and the low-moves warning.

### Getting out of the way

When a video ad plays, the game's music goes **all the way down**, not just quieter. Music and an advert's own audio playing at once was one of the first things we fixed. Sound effects are left as they are.

One bug came only from real hardware: the iPhone's silent switch muted the whole game, because of the audio category Unity uses by default. The game now uses the category for apps whose sound is the point. And one honest note from our own playtesting is still open: "audio sounds are okay but not good". There is more to do here, and we know it.

There is one speaker toggle in settings, for music and effects together, and it is remembered with your progress.

## Why the first version has no vibration

Most polished mobile games use haptics: small, crisp taps from the phone's vibration motor that make a pour or a completed jar feel physical. SpiceCraft's first version ships without them, and the reason is the most "us" decision in this post.

**Nothing in our process can check them.**

Every other part of game feel in this post is verified the same way: build the game, put it on a phone or the iPhone simulator, and look, listen or measure. Haptics break that loop. The iPhone simulator has no vibration motor, and calls to it are silently ignored. A haptic bug, such as a buzz on the wrong beat, a buzz that is too strong or no buzz at all, would be completely invisible to us.

The options were not great either. Unity's built-in vibration is a flat one-second buzz, which is worse than nothing. The best-known Unity haptics plugin had been archived and needed an input system we had decided not to use, and the newer alternative was very young. Writing our own is around a hundred lines of native code, which is small, but unverifiable code is unverifiable however short it is.

So we wrote down what would reverse the decision: **a physical iPhone in the testing loop.** We also wrote down what we would build when that happens, so the decision does not have to be re-made from scratch. Haptics on just four beats (the cork seating, the pour, the jar landing and a jar completing), and never on a refused tap.

Shipping without a feature we cannot verify felt better than shipping one we could only hope was right.

## What we learned

1. **Turn feel into numbers where you can.** A colour-difference floor, a loudness map and a frame-time target are all things a test can hold.
2. **Use the measure that matches people.** CIE76 told us our closest colours were safe and pointed us at the wrong pairs.
3. **Measure what is drawn, not what is assigned.** Transparency closed a 20.2 gap to 15.1, and a test of the assigned colours passed with the bug in.
4. **Check that a test can fail.** A test reading the same constant it was meant to check passed with the floor at a third of its value.
5. **Listen to the quietest sound you play most often.** Ours was 8 dB under the music.
6. **Do not ship what you cannot verify.** No haptics until a real phone is in the loop, and the plan for that day is already written.

SpiceCraft is free on [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.spicecraft), and the iPhone version is coming soon. Play it with the sound on.

The full series: [why our first game is a sort puzzle](/blog/why-our-first-game-is-a-sort-puzzle), [200 levels, every one solvable](/blog/spicecraft-200-levels-every-one-solvable), [room for mistakes](/blog/spicecraft-room-for-mistakes-move-budget-and-hints), [the prototype is the specification](/blog/spicecraft-prototype-is-the-specification), and this post.
